title: Naya Raasta (Sarg 1-13)
tagline: The prescribed novel to Sarg 13: its reported story, its people, its themes, and how to study and answer on it.

overview.intro: Naya Raasta by Sushma Agarwal is the novel prescribed for ICSE Class IX Hindi, and it is the book the prescribed-books appendix divides between the two years: Sarg 1 to Sarg 13 for Class IX and Sarg 14 to Sarg 26 for Class X. The novel itself stays in your prescribed textbook; this chapter does not reproduce a line of it. What it offers is a study frame built from published summaries, reviews and guide material — the reported shape of the story, the people the summaries name, the themes an answer turns on, and a method for reading the prescribed units and writing about them with confidence. Every account of events below rests on that secondary authority and is introduced on it, and the final lesson shows you how to check each detail against your own copy before you commit it to an answer.

learn.title: What is prescribed, and how this chapter is grounded

blocks.text: The ICSE Hindi syllabus prescribes a novel alongside the Sahitya Sagar stories and poems, and the prescribed-books appendix for Examination Year 2028 lists Naya Raasta by Sushma Agarwal and divides it between the two years: Sarg 1 to Sarg 13 form the Class IX portion, and Sarg 14 to Sarg 26 follow for Class X. Study materials variously call these instalments sarg or adhyay, so the numbering printed in your own edition is the final authority on where one unit ends and the next begins. Because the novel is a copyrighted book, this chapter reproduces none of its text: every account of events below follows published summaries and study guides, and each is introduced on that authority rather than as a quotation from the novel.

What that means for you as a reader is a division of labour. Read the prescribed units in your own copy of the novel first, because the novel is the only authority for what happens in it. Use this chapter afterwards to organise what you read: a clear map of the people, a list of the reported events in order, a frame for the themes, and a method for turning all three into written answers. Any line you intend to quote and any detail you intend to state as fact should be confirmed in your edition before you write it — summaries compress, reorder and occasionally disagree on minor names, and an answer built on a detail your book does not contain is an avoidable risk.

learn.title: The story as published summaries report it

blocks.text: Published summaries describe Meenu as a capable, academically successful young woman in a middle-class family, and they are careful to say that her abilities are recognised at home even while her marriage prospects keep failing. The reported reasons for those failures are the usual ones that the novel is read for: prospective grooms judge her complexion and weigh the question of dowry, so meetings happen and then stop happening. The situation changes when Mayaram and his son Amit come to meet her — the summaries say that Amit likes her — and it changes again at Mayaram’s home, where the wealthy Dhanimal proposes his daughter Sarita for Amit and is reported to offer a large contribution, given as five lakh rupees in the summaries, towards the wedding expenses.

items: As the summaries report it, Meenu’s abilities and education are praised in her own household while prospective grooms reject her on the grounds of complexion and dowry.
Mayaram and his son Amit visit the family, and Amit’s favourable impression of Meenu is reported by every summary that covers the episode.
At home, Dhanimal proposes his daughter Sarita for Amit, and the reported contribution of five lakh rupees towards the wedding makes the match attractive to Mayaram’s wife.
To avoid a direct refusal of Meenu’s family, Mayaram’s wife is reported to suggest that the younger sister Asha be given instead, expecting the proposal to be declined.
Meenu’s father, Dayaram, later learns that the match for Amit is being fixed with Sarita — the discovery that the summaries present as the turning of the family’s position.

blocks.text: Read that sequence as a map rather than as the text. Summaries compress whole episodes into a sentence, and two of them may order the same events differently or differ on a minor name; what they agree on is the structure of the situation. A family is visited by a match it welcomes; a wealthier counter-proposal is made behind the scenes; a manoeuvre is used to avoid an open refusal; and the truth reaches the father too late for comfort. Hold that structure and you can rebuild the details from your own reading, which is exactly the habit an answer on a prescribed novel needs.

learn.title: Meenu’s choice and the reported shape of the novel

blocks.text: The refusal does not end Meenu’s story; it redirects it, and this is where the novel earns its title. Published summaries report that she decides not to pursue marriage and instead takes up law, an ambition she had held since childhood. Her parents allow it, and the summaries say that she qualifies and becomes a successful practising lawyer. The reported line of the story then widens: the marriage to Sarita does not go ahead, Amit remains unhappy about the way the earlier match was handled, and later he is injured in an accident. Meenu hears about it through her friend Neelima and visits him in hospital, and the summaries describe that visit as the point at which the bitterness between the two begins to ease.

items: Meenu chooses study over the marriage that has been negotiated away — the first and defining turn towards the new path.
She qualifies in law and practises, so the choice becomes a standing of her own rather than a protest.
The reported marriage to Sarita does not proceed, and Amit is said to remain unhappy about the handling of the earlier match.
After Amit’s accident and Meenu’s hospital visit, the reported misunderstanding between the families eases.
Mayaram is said to apologise to Dayaram and to propose Meenu’s marriage to Amit, which she agrees to — summaries end with her married and still the lawyer she has become.

blocks.text: The title, naya raasta, means the new path, and the reported shape of the story gives it two connected steps. The first is the turn from marriage negotiations to study, qualification and a profession — a way of life built on learning and earning. The second is the later agreement to marriage entered from that new standing, on changed terms and after the family’s apology, rather than under the pressure that attended the first match. Because of the second step, resist the easy reading that sets marriage and independence against each other as clean opposites: the summaries hold both together, and a strong answer defines the new path as a change in Meenu’s position and agency rather than as the rejection of one thing in favour of another.

learn.title: The people, as the summaries name them

items.meaning: The central character: capable and academically successful, rejected in marriage on the reported grounds of appearance and dowry, and the one who turns to law and a career of her own.
Mayaram’s son, who is reported to like Meenu when his family visits, remains unhappy when the match is redirected, and later renews contact after his accident.
Meenu’s father, who receives the reported proposal for his daughter and later learns that Amit’s match is being fixed with Sarita.
Meenu’s younger sister, named in the reported manoeuvre by which Mayaram’s wife expects to avoid the match without an open refusal.
Amit’s father, host of the visit to Meenu’s family; in the reported ending he apologises to Dayaram and proposes the marriage afresh.
The wealthy man who proposes his daughter Sarita for Amit and is reported to offer a large contribution towards the wedding expenses.
Dhanimal’s daughter, proposed for Amit in the reported counter-match that helps end the earlier arrangement.
Meenu’s friend, through whom the news of Amit’s accident reaches Meenu and the hospital visit becomes possible.

blocks.text: Fix every relationship from your own edition before you build an answer on it. The study materials that summarise this novel do not always agree on the minor figures: one guide labels a relative as Meenu’s sister where another makes her Mayaram’s daughter, and the two families each have members whom some lists name and others leave out. The central figures — Meenu, Amit, Dayaram, Mayaram, Dhanimal, Sarita — recur consistently across summaries, so an answer anchored on them is safe; the periphery is where guides diverge, and that is precisely the material worth a minute with your prescribed copy before the examination.

learn.title: The themes an answer is built on

blocks.caption: Reported events turned into theme points
columns: How the reported events show it
rows: Marriage, family expectation and dowry

blocks.text: Themes are not slogans that a novel happens to contain; they are arguments that reported events are made to support. Take appearance and worth as the model: the reported rejections judge Meenu by complexion and by what a family must pay, while the same summaries insist on her academic and domestic abilities — and later, her qualification in law. That contrast is the evidence, and the argument is that the novel measures a woman twice and finds the first measure wanting. Build each of the other themes the same way: name the reported events, say what they show, and only then step up to the general claim about society that the question is really asking for.

learn.title: Reading unit by unit, and answering safely

items: Read one prescribed unit in your edition and close the book before noting: three lines on the events, two on the people who appear, one on the theme it advances.
Compare your notes with the map in this chapter, and mark any difference in order or naming — the difference is where your edition is right and the summary is not.
Keep a running list of names with their relationships on one page, confirmed from the novel, because guides disagree precisely on this material.
Answer one practice question per unit without looking at your notes, then check and add only what you missed — recall with a check beats rereading without one.
Before writing any quotation, find it in your edition; write it in your own words if you cannot, since a misquotation costs more than a paraphrase.

blocks.text: The questions this novel invites come in a few recognisable shapes. Study materials ask for character sketches — Meenu above all, then the men whose decisions shape her situation — for the significance of the title, for value-based answers on dowry and on a woman’s self-reliance, and for objective items on reported plot facts: who proposed which match, whose daughter is whom, who brings the news of the accident. Section B of the paper asks four questions drawn from the two prescribed texts, so breadth across the whole Class IX portion matters as much as depth on a favourite episode; a student who has prepared three units well and read none of the rest walks into that section with half its material closed.

items.text: Weak: “Meenu was a very brave girl. She faced everything bravely and finally succeeded.”
items.note: Adjectives without events. The reader learns what you think of Meenu but nothing that happened, so nothing can be verified or awarded.

items.text: Strong: “Meenu’s bravery is visible in her response to the failed match: instead of accepting the judgment, she returns to law, qualifies and practises.”
items.note: Trait, reported event and consequence in one sentence — and it can be checked against the prescribed units before submission.

keyPoints: The prescribed novel is Naya Raasta by Sushma Agarwal; the Class IX portion is Sarg 1 to Sarg 13, recorded in the Examination Year 2028 Appendix I as reproduced in published mirrors.
This chapter reproduces no text of the novel: its account of events follows published summaries and must be confirmed against your prescribed edition.
As summaries report it, Meenu’s proposed marriage fails on the grounds of appearance and dowry, and her family learns the match was redirected to Sarita.
The reported counter-match runs through Dhanimal, who proposes his daughter Sarita for Amit with a stated contribution towards the wedding.
Meenu’s response, as reported, is to study law — an ambition held since childhood — and to qualify and practise successfully.
The reported ending holds both choices together: Meenu becomes a lawyer and later agrees to marry Amit after Mayaram’s apology.
Themes to prepare: marriage and family expectation, appearance and worth, education and self-reliance, and choice against circumstance.
Study guides disagree about some minor relationships, so confirm every name and relation in your own copy before quoting it.
Section B asks four questions from the two prescribed texts, so the whole Class IX portion must be read, not a single favourite episode.
examFocus: Title question: define the “new path” in one sentence of your own, then support it with the reported sequence — refusal, study of law, profession, later agreement.
Character sketch: prepare Meenu most fully; build the sketch from ability, response to rejection, decision and achievement, each tied to a verified episode.
Value question: dowry and the weighing of a person against money — argue from the two reported proposals rather than from generalities.
Event questions: know the order — the visit, the proposal through Dhanimal, the Asha alternative, the father’s discovery, the decision, the accident, the apology.
Objective facts: whose daughter Sarita is, who proposes which match, who carries the news of the accident — the items study materials test most often.
Never present a summary’s detail as a quotation from the novel: state events in your own words after checking them, and reserve quotation for lines you have found.

questions.prompt: Which novel is prescribed for ICSE Class IX Hindi, and who wrote it?
options: Wah Janmabhoomi Meri by Sohanlal Dwivedi
questions.explanation: The Examination Year 2028 prescribed-books appendix lists Naya Raasta by Sushma Agarwal as the Class IX novel. Sahitya Sagar supplies the short stories and poems, and the other two titles are individual selections from it rather than the novel.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing a Sahitya Sagar title because it is also prescribed — those are the story and poem selections, not the novel.

questions.prompt: According to published summaries, what does Meenu do after the marriage arrangement fails?
options: She takes up the study of law and builds a career
She agrees at once to marry Amit
She leaves school and returns to her village
questions.answer: She takes up the study of law and builds a career
questions.explanation: The summaries report that Meenu decides not to pursue marriage and instead pursues law, an ambition held since childhood; her parents allow it and she qualifies and practises. The other options contradict the reported sequence of events.
questions.commonMistake: Placing the marriage first and the career afterwards — the reported order is the reverse, and the order is the point of the title.

questions.prompt: In the reported story, why does the proposed match between Amit and Meenu not go ahead?
options: A wealthier match for Amit is arranged with Sarita
Amit refuses to meet Meenu’s family
Meenu’s family demands a larger dowry
The two families live in different cities
questions.answer: A wealthier match for Amit is arranged with Sarita
questions.explanation: The summaries say Amit likes Meenu, but at home Dhanimal proposes his daughter Sarita for Amit with a reported contribution to the wedding, and Mayaram’s wife favours that wealthy match. The refusal that follows comes from that shift, not from any demand by Meenu’s family.
questions.commonMistake: Blaming Meenu’s family for the collapse — the reported initiative lies with the wealthier proposal on Amit’s side.

questions.prompt: Who is Sarita, according to published summaries?
questions.explanation: Summaries identify Sarita as the daughter of the wealthy Dhanimal, whose proposal for Amit is the reported reason the earlier match with Meenu is dropped. Keeping the two fathers and their children straight is one of the commonest confusions in this novel.
questions.commonMistake: Mixing up the families — Sarita belongs to Dhanimal’s side, while Asha is Meenu’s younger sister.

questions.prompt: Complete: the Class IX portion of the prescribed novel runs from Sarg ____ to Sarg ____, while the later units are prescribed for Class X.
questions.explanation: The Examination Year 2028 appendix, as reproduced in published mirrors, allocates Sarg 1 to Sarg 13 to Class IX and Sarg 14 to Sarg 26 to Class X. Study materials call these units sarg or adhyay, so confirm the numbering in your own edition as well.
questions.commonMistake: Starting the Class IX portion at the far end of the novel, or forgetting that the split runs from the beginning rather than to it.

questions.prompt: According to published summaries, what is the “new path” that the novel’s title points to?
questions.answer: The path Meenu chooses when the reported match collapses: she turns away from pursuing marriage and takes up the study of law, and the summaries follow her to qualification and a practice of her own — a life built on learning and earning rather than on the marriage her family had been arranging.
questions.explanation: The title question wants the path defined rather than the plot retold. Name the change of direction first — from marriage negotiations to study and a profession — and then show that it is a change of standing, because the summaries say she qualifies and practises.
questions.commonMistake: Answering only that she refused to marry: without the profession there is a refusal, not a path.

questions.prompt: Who is Neelima, and what does she bring about in the reported account?
questions.answer: Neelima is described as Meenu’s friend. In the reported account she is the link through which Meenu hears of Amit’s accident and goes to see him in hospital, and that visit is the point at which the bitterness between the two begins to ease.
questions.explanation: Neelima has a small but structural role: she carries the news that restarts contact between the two families. An answer that stops at naming her describes her presence but not her function in the reported sequence.
questions.commonMistake: Making Neelima a sister or the person who proposes the marriage — the summaries cast her as a friend and a messenger.

questions.prompt: Retell, on the authority of published summaries, how the proposed marriage fails and what Meenu decides instead.
questions.answer: Summaries report that Meenu is a capable, academically successful young woman whose marriage prospects nevertheless keep failing, particularly because of her complexion and the question of dowry. When Mayaram and his son Amit come to meet her, Amit likes her; but at home the wealthy Dhanimal proposes his daughter Sarita for Amit and is reported to offer five lakh rupees towards the wedding, and Mayaram’s wife favours this wealthy match. To avoid a direct refusal she suggests that Meenu’s family instead give the younger sister Asha, expecting the proposal to be declined; Meenu’s father Dayaram later learns that Amit’s match is being fixed with Sarita. Faced with this, Meenu decides not to pursue marriage. She takes up law, the career she had wanted since childhood; her parents allow it, and she qualifies and becomes a practising lawyer. The account is the summaries’ report of events and should be checked against the prescribed units before any detail is stated as fact.
questions.explanation: The marks sit in sequence and attribution: the failed prospects, the visit, the wealthy counter-proposal, the Asha manoeuvre, the father’s discovery, the decision, the qualification. Write the chain in order and name your authority at the end, because the question itself asks for the summaries’ account.
questions.commonMistake: Dropping the Asha proposal — the hinge of the family’s manoeuvre — or telling the story as unquestioned fact without naming where it comes from.

questions.prompt: A study guide asks: “Can Naya Raasta be read as a novel about choice rather than only about marriage?” Answer from the reported events, and state what you must verify before quoting.
questions.answer: Yes, and the reported events support both readings at once. Marriage supplies the occasions: a match that fails on the grounds of appearance and dowry, a wealthier match preferred for Amit, and a later agreement to marry on entirely changed terms. Choice supplies the structure: Meenu answers rejection by choosing law and a profession, chooses to see Amit when contact is renewed through Neelima, and finally agrees to a marriage entered from a position of qualification and standing rather than of family pressure. The two readings must be held together rather than played against each other, since the reported ending gives her both a profession and a marriage. Before quoting anything, verify in your own edition the order of the units, the names and relationships of the minor characters, and any line you intend to reproduce — summaries compress and reorder, and two of them may disagree on a single detail.
questions.explanation: An analytical answer takes a position, proves it with the reported sequence, and then handles the counter-reading instead of ignoring it. The verification sentence is not decoration: a question about the novel’s scope invites exactly the over-claim that checking prevents.
questions.commonMistake: Reducing the novel to a clean either-or between marriage and independence, which the reported ending does not support.

questions.prompt: Write a character sketch of Meenu as published summaries present her, and mark the details you would confirm against your prescribed edition.
questions.answer: As published summaries present her, Meenu is capable and academically successful in a middle-class family, and her abilities are praised at home even while prospective grooms reject her on the grounds of her complexion and the dowry question. Her defining response to that rejection is not despair but redirection: she returns to an ambition held since childhood, studies law, and the summaries say she qualifies and practises successfully. Later she chooses to visit Amit when she hears of his accident through Neelima, and agrees to the renewed match — choices made from a position she built herself. Her portrait therefore gathers determination, learning and steadiness under pressure. Details to confirm in the prescribed copy before quoting: the order of the visits and proposals, the names and relationships of the minor characters, since guides disagree about some, the figure reported towards the wedding expenses, and any sentence reproduced verbatim.
questions.explanation: A character sketch earns its marks from traits proved by episodes, so give the trait, then the reported event that shows it, in order. The final instruction about verification belongs to the same discipline: a sketch built on a guide’s error about a relationship is wrong even when it reads well.
questions.commonMistake: Filling the sketch with adjectives and no events, or treating a guidebook’s minor-name as the novel’s own.
